Why it works: Bat bites can be tiny and unnoticed, and rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start. Treatment given soon after exposure prevents the disease. Capturing the bat safely allows testing, which may remove the need for treatment.

Example: A mother finds a bat in her child's room. She keeps the door shut, calls the local health department, and follows their advice about capture and testing.

Apply it today: Save your local health department's number, and learn wound care at a hands-on first aid course.

source.title: Rabies: Bats
source.author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

ideas.title: Make a favorite activity the reward for a dull one
ideas.body: Psychologist David Premack observed that a more probable behavior can reinforce a less probable one. In plain terms: do the thing you do not want to do first, and let the thing you do want to do follow it.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Access to a preferred activity acts as a reward. This works with whatever you already choose freely, so it needs no outside incentive. The order matters: the pleasant activity is only available after the less pleasant one.

Example: A parent says, once the homework is done, you can play the game. The same applies to an adult who allows a favorite podcast or a coffee only after an hour of the harder task.

Apply it today: Pick a task you are avoiding and decide on a specific thing you enjoy that you will allow only after it. Tell yourself the rule before you start.

ideas.title: Texting money through corner shops reached people banks ignored
ideas.body: M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007. Customers deposit cash with a local agent, who credits their phone account, and then send money by text message. Many people without bank accounts could pay bills and send money to relatives.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Mobile phones spread faster than branches. Agents like shop owners acted as the cash-in, cash-out points. Sending money to family far away became quick and cheap compared with buses or couriers.

Example: A study published in Science found that the spread of the service helped some Kenyan households, especially those headed by women, escape poverty. Researchers credited easier saving and better ways to cope with shocks.

Apply it today: Next time you send money, check the fee and time involved, and compare with an alternative route you know.

ideas.title: Notice who does the work that does not lead to promotion
ideas.body: Every team has tasks that matter but do not help careers, such as taking notes, planning parties or training new hires. In experiments, women were more likely than men to volunteer for such tasks and to be asked to do them.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: If the same people take the unrewarded work, they lose time for the work that brings promotion. The researchers showed this in a lab setting with money at stake, so the pattern is not just a matter of opinion. Rotating the tasks spreads the burden.

Example: A team keeps asking the same colleague to take minutes. A simple rota would give everyone a turn and leave her time for the project that gets noticed.

Apply it today: Look at who does the low-visibility tasks on your team, and suggest a rotating list at the next meeting.

source.title: Gender differences in accepting and receiving requests for tasks with low promotability
source.author: Linda Babcock, Maria P. Recalde, Lise Vesterlund and Laurie Weingart

ideas.title: Cool leftovers within two hours and reheat them until steaming hot
ideas.body: Put cooked food in the fridge within two hours, one hour if it is very hot out. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot all the way through, and use a thermometer to check they reach 165 degrees Fahrenheit.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Bacteria multiply rapidly in the danger zone between cold and hot temperatures, and some produce toxins that reheating does not destroy. Quick chilling stops growth. Reheating kills most germs that have started to grow.

Example: After a party a host leaves the pasta out overnight. In the morning she throws it away instead of reheating it. A better habit is to portion leftovers into shallow containers and refrigerate them soon after eating.

Apply it today: Check your fridge temperature today.

source.title: Leftovers and Food Safety
source.author: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service

ideas.title: Unpredictable rewards keep you checking
ideas.body: B. F. Skinner and Charles Ferster studied schedules of reinforcement. Rewards that arrive unpredictably, after a varying number of responses, produce steady, persistent behavior that is hard to extinguish. Slot machines work this way.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: When you cannot tell which attempt will pay off, every attempt feels like it might be the one. Predictable rewards allow you to stop once you have collected. Unpredictable ones keep you going. Many apps use feeds and notifications in a similar way.

Example: Refreshing an inbox or feed pays out something interesting only now and then, and you cannot tell when. That uncertainty keeps the checking habit strong, even when most checks yield nothing.

Apply it today: Turn off one notification today, and check that app at set times instead. Watch how often the urge arrives with nothing new waiting.

source.title: Schedules of Reinforcement
source.author: Charles B. Ferster and B. F. Skinner

ideas.title: Aid works better when you test it like medicine
ideas.body: Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo argue that poverty programs should be tested with randomized trials: some villages get an idea and others do not. In one Indian study, giving families a bag of lentils for vaccinating their children raised immunisation rates.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Random assignment creates comparable groups, so differences can be credited to the program. Without it, richer or more motivated villages may look better for other reasons. Small, practical questions can be answered with evidence.

Example: The lentils worked because they lowered a hidden cost, a trip to a distant clinic, and made the benefit immediate. Their work, with Michael Kremer, earned the 2019 Nobel Prize in economics.

Apply it today: Pick one habit or change you want to try, and design a simple test with a fair comparison, such as two weeks with and two weeks without.

source.title: Poor Economics
source.author: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo

ideas.title: Asking for a small favor can make someone like you more
ideas.body: In a classic experiment, people who did a favor for a researcher liked him more than people who were not asked. We tend to believe we did the favor because we like the person, so we like them more.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Behavior shapes attitudes: if we help someone, we justify it by thinking well of them. This is sometimes named after a story Benjamin Franklin told about winning over a rival by asking to borrow a book. Keep the favor small and easy.

Example: A new colleague asks a neighbor in the next cubicle to recommend a good lunch place. The neighbor enjoys being helpful, and they start having lunch together.

Apply it today: Ask someone you want to know better for a small piece of advice or help, and thank them clearly afterward.

source.title: Liking a person as a function of doing him a favour
source.author: Jon E. Jecker and David Landy

ideas.title: Build a first aid kit, check it twice a year and learn what is in it
ideas.body: A basic kit should include adhesive bandages, gauze, tape, gloves, tweezers, a thermometer, and any personal medicines. Keep one at home and one in the car, and check expiry dates twice a year.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A kit only helps if it is stocked, close at hand and understood. Expired or missing items are a common problem. Tailoring it to your household, such as an epinephrine auto-injector for allergies, matters most.

Example: A family opens the kit before a camping trip and finds the plasters are gone and the creams have expired. They restock, add a small card with emergency numbers and tuck it into the car.

Apply it today: Open your kit this weekend, replace what is missing, and Take a hands-on first aid course from the Red Cross, St John Ambulance or a local provider, so your hands know what to do.

source.title: First-aid kits: Stock supplies that can save lives
source.author: Mayo Clinic

ideas.title: Be nice, retaliate once, forgive, and stay clear
ideas.body: Robert Axelrod ran tournaments in which programs played the repeated prisoner's dilemma. The simple winner, Tit for Tat, started by cooperating and then copied the opponent's last move. It was friendly, firm, forgiving and clear.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: In repeated dealings, cooperation pays because the future matters. Starting kind invites trust, answering betrayal discourages exploitation, and forgiving ends cycles of revenge. A strategy that others can easily read makes cooperation easier to keep going.

Example: Two businesses that trade regularly can reach a good working relationship by starting in good faith, pushing back once if one misses a delivery, and then returning to normal when the other corrects it.

Apply it today: In your next repeated relationship, such as a flatmate or coworker, start generous, respond calmly once to a slip, and then return to goodwill when they do.

ideas.title: Too many owners with a veto can leave a resource unused
ideas.body: Michael Heller named the tragedy of the anticommons: when many people can each block use of a resource, it sits idle. His example was Moscow after the Soviet era, where storefronts stayed empty while kiosks lined the street, since too many parties had to agree.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: The commons problem is overuse, the anticommons is underuse. When rights are split among many holders, each can hold out for more, and deals become too costly. A single owner could simply decide.

Example: Researchers have used the idea to discuss drug development and patents, where many overlapping patents may slow work, and land with many heirs who cannot agree. Evidence on how large the effect is varies by case.

Apply it today: If a project of yours is stuck, count how many people have to say yes, and see if you can cut the number.

source.title: The Tragedy of the Anticommons: Property in the Transition from Marx to Markets
source.author: Michael A. Heller

ideas.title: Be warm and firm at once with children
ideas.body: Psychologist Diana Baumrind described an authoritative style: high warmth and clear expectations, with reasons given for rules. Children raised this way tend to do better in school and behavior than with harsh or permissive styles.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Warmth makes a child willing to listen, and structure gives security and guidance. Harshness without warmth breeds fear, while warmth without limits leaves children without guidance. The research is mostly correlational, but the pattern is consistent.

Example: A child throws her coat on the floor. A parent in this style says calmly that coats go on the hook because it keeps the hall clear, and waits while she does it, without shouting or giving in.

Apply it today: Next time you set a limit, give a one-sentence reason and say something kind about the child in the same breath.

ideas.title: For hypothermia, handle gently, remove wet clothes and warm the trunk
ideas.body: If someone is shivering badly, confused or clumsy from cold, call emergency services. Move them somewhere sheltered, remove wet clothing, wrap them in blankets and insulate them from the ground. Warm the chest and trunk first.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Cold slows the body and brain, and the heart becomes sensitive to rough movement. Warming the core first protects the vital organs. Hot baths and rubbing the limbs can do harm.

Example: A walker is found cold and confused beside a stream. A companion calls for help, replaces his wet jacket with a dry layer, wraps him in a sleeping bag and gives warm sweet drinks only if he is alert.

Apply it today: Pack a spare insulating layer and a foil blanket, and Take a hands-on first aid course from the Red Cross, St John Ambulance or a local provider, so your hands know what to do.

ideas.title: Shared resources can be protected without selling or policing them
ideas.body: Elinor Ostrom studied communities that managed shared resources such as fisheries, forests and irrigation systems. She found many succeeded without privatization or top-down control, when they had suitable rules. She won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Ostrom found that successful groups tended to have clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, a say for users in changing them, monitoring, and graduated penalties. This challenged the idea that overuse of shared resources is inevitable.

Example: A neighborhood that shares a garden or a flatshare that shares supplies can avoid overuse by agreeing on rules, tracking use and giving small, fair responses to those who break them.

Apply it today: If you share a resource with others, such as a drive or a fridge, propose three simple rules and a way to check them. Agree on what happens when someone breaks a rule.

source.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
source.author: Elinor Ostrom

ideas.title: Years of failed experiments taught mRNA not to trigger alarms
ideas.body: Katalin Kariko and Drew Weissman found that swapping a letter of synthetic mRNA for a modified one stopped the body's immune system from attacking it. That cleared the way for mRNA vaccines. They won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Cells read mRNA as instructions for making a protein. Unmodified lab-made mRNA looked like an invader and caused inflammation. The modification made it look like the body's own. Delivery in small fat bubbles protected it on the way.

Example: Their work from the 2000s was met with limited funding for years. The same approach allowed vaccines against COVID-19 to be made within a year of the virus's sequence being published.

Apply it today: Read one short Nobel Prize summary of this work, and note how long it took between the first finding and its use.

source.title: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023 (NobelPrize.org)

ideas.title: A joke or a soft touch mid-argument can stop it spiraling
ideas.body: John Gottman calls them repair attempts: small gestures that stop tension from rising, such as humor, a pause, or saying: I am sorry, let me start again. Whether they work depends on how the other person receives them.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Gottman's studies of couples found that successful couples make repair attempts and accept them, while troubled couples ignore them. A repair works when the relationship is healthy enough that the other person reads it as an offer of peace.

Example: In the middle of an argument about chores, one partner says, we are both tired, can we try again? The other smiles and accepts, and the tone drops at once.

Apply it today: Choose a phrase you can use mid-argument, such as: can we take a breath? Agree with your partner that when either says it, you both pause.

source.title: Why Marriages Succeed or Fail
source.author: John M. Gottman and Nan Silver

ideas.title: Charge your phone before a storm and switch on low power mode
ideas.body: When bad weather is forecast, charge your phone and power bank, turn on low power mode, and dim the screen. Use text messages rather than calls to save battery and keep networks free for emergency use.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: After a disaster, power may be out for days and phone batteries are your main connection to alerts and family. Texting uses less power and network capacity than calls. A charged power bank can extend your phone for days.

Example: Before a storm, a family charges every device, saves emergency numbers on paper, and agrees to send a single text to the out-of-town contact each evening.

Apply it today: Charge a power bank and store it with your emergency kit.

ideas.title: Without talking, people converge on the obvious choice
ideas.body: Thomas Schelling asked people where they would go to meet a stranger in New York with no way to communicate and no set place or time. Many picked the same spot. Such focal points let us coordinate without a word.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: When talking is impossible, people look for the option that stands out as prominent or natural, and expect others to do the same. Uniqueness and convention make a choice focal. This explains why people coordinate on traditions and landmarks.

Example: If you and a friend get separated in a large festival with no phone signal, you are likelier to find each other at the main entrance or the biggest stage than anywhere random.

Apply it today: Agree with your family or team on one fallback meeting place and one fallback time in case your plans fall through. Write them down today.

ideas.title: Singapore turns used water into drinking-quality water
ideas.body: Singapore treats wastewater with membrane filtering, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet light to make water it calls NEWater. Most of it goes to industry, and a small portion is added to reservoirs. The city-state has few natural water sources.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Reverse osmosis pushes water through a membrane that blocks salts and most contaminants. Followed by ultraviolet disinfection, the result is very clean. Public acceptance was built through education and by having leaders drink it.

Example: Singapore has used it since the early 2000s, with plans to meet more of its needs this way. Other dry regions, such as parts of California, run similar reuse programs.

Apply it today: Find out where your tap water comes from and what happens to it after you flush.

ideas.title: People who eat with others more often tend to feel closer to them
ideas.body: A UK survey found that people who ate socially more often felt happier and more satisfied with life and had more friends to count on. It was a survey, so the link may run both ways.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Shared meals give regular, relaxed time together and a natural reason to talk. The study could not show that eating together causes these outcomes. Still, a meal is an easy habit and takes no extra time.

Example: A group of coworkers who eat lunch together once a week learn about each other's lives, and when one is stressed, the others notice.

Apply it today: Invite one person to share a meal this week, even a simple one, and put it on the calendar.

source.title: Breaking bread: the functions of social eating
source.author: Robin I. M. Dunbar

ideas.title: Good Samaritan laws protect people who give reasonable help
ideas.body: Many places have Good Samaritan laws that protect people who give emergency help in good faith from legal liability. The details vary by location, but the aim is to remove the fear of being sued from the decision to help.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Fear of legal trouble is one reason bystanders hesitate. These laws generally cover those who act reasonably and without payment, and they do not cover gross negligence. Knowing the principle helps you act, though you should check the rules where you live.

Example: A passer-by sees a driver slumped at the wheel. He hesitates, remembers that the law in his region protects honest help, calls emergency services and starts first aid.

Apply it today: Look up the Good Samaritan rule where you live, and Take a hands-on first aid course from the Red Cross, St John Ambulance or a local provider, so your hands know what to do.

ideas.title: Experts see few possibilities, beginners see many
ideas.body: Zen teacher Shunryu Suzuki described the beginner's mind: an open, eager attitude free of fixed ideas. In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities, he said, while in the expert's mind there are few.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Expertise helps you act fast but also fixes your assumptions. Approaching a familiar thing as if for the first time brings back questions you stopped asking. It is not a call to ignore what you know, but to hold it loosely.

Example: A veteran technician with a recurring fault may assume the usual cause. A new colleague asks a naive question that leads to the real one. Both views are useful.

Apply it today: Take a task you do on autopilot and do it as if teaching it to a newcomer. Notice one step you have never questioned and ask why it is done that way.

ideas.title: One banker locked rivals in a library to stop a financial panic
ideas.body: In October 1907, trust companies in New York faced runs. J. P. Morgan gathered bankers in his library and reportedly kept them there until they agreed on a rescue fund. The panic eased, and the episode helped lead to the Federal Reserve Act in 1913.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: With no central bank, the country relied on private figures to supply emergency cash. That worked only because one person had both money and trust. It showed the need for a permanent institution able to lend in a crisis.

Example: The Fed was set up to provide an elastic currency and a lender of last resort. Many details of the story are told differently, but the broad outline of Morgan's role is well documented.

Apply it today: Look up who in your country can lend to banks in an emergency, and when that institution was created.

ideas.title: The best support is often the kind the receiver does not notice
ideas.body: In a study of couples in which one partner was preparing for a major exam, the stressed partner did better when the other gave support the receiver did not notice, such as quietly taking on chores.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Overt help can imply the person cannot cope, which adds to their stress. Invisible support helps without that cost. In the study, the stressed partner's anxiety fell most when help arrived without being flagged.

Example: A student is swamped before finals. Her roommate cleans the kitchen and says nothing. She simply finds the task done and has the time she needed.

Apply it today: Do one thing for someone under pressure today without announcing it, such as taking on a chore.

source.title: Invisible support and adjustment to stress
source.author: Niall Bolger, Adam Zuckerman and Ronald C. Kessler

ideas.title: Know your evacuation zone before the storm season starts
ideas.body: Coastal areas are divided into evacuation zones based on storm surge risk. Look up your zone, know the route and destination you would use, and leave when officials tell your zone to go.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Orders are issued by zone so that the roads are not overwhelmed and the people at greatest risk leave first. Knowing your zone ahead of time removes confusion during a stressful event. Surge is the main killer in hurricanes.

Example: A family looks up their zone in June and finds they are in a high-risk area. They plan a route inland and a place to stay. When the order comes, they leave early.

Apply it today: Find your zone on your local emergency management website, and join a local preparedness class for hands-on practice.

ideas.title: People prefer known odds to unknown odds, even when the unknown is no worse
ideas.body: Daniel Ellsberg showed that people prefer to bet on an urn with a known mix of colors rather than one with an unknown mix, even when there is no reason to think the unknown mix is worse. This is ambiguity aversion.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Not knowing the odds feels more uncomfortable than facing known risk, and people avoid it even at a cost. Yet in real life, odds are often unknown, and refusing every uncertain option can mean passing up good ones.

Example: A person turns down a new job because its prospects are unclear, and takes a familiar one with a slightly worse outlook, simply because the odds of the old one feel known.

Apply it today: Next time you reject an option for being uncertain, ask whether you are rejecting it for being risky or only for being unfamiliar. Try to put a rough range on it.

source.title: Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms
source.author: Daniel Ellsberg

ideas.title: In a panic, lend freely, at a high rate, against good collateral
ideas.body: Walter Bagehot's 1873 book Lombard Street set out a rule for central banks: in a crisis, lend without limit to solvent firms, at a penalty rate, against good security. The aim is to stop panic without rewarding recklessness.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: A bank that is sound but short of cash can be driven under by a run. Lending freely lets it pay depositors and calm fear. A high rate and good collateral keep borrowers from using the help except when they truly need it.

Example: Central banks followed this approach in 2008 and again in 2020, opening emergency lending lines. Critics argue about what counts as good collateral and who is solvent, which can be hard to judge in the middle of a panic.

Apply it today: When you read about a bank rescue, check whether it matches Bagehot's three conditions.

source.title: Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market
source.author: Walter Bagehot

ideas.title: Holiday relaxation fades within weeks, so rest in small doses all year
ideas.body: A review of vacation studies found that gains in health and well-being from time off faded within a few weeks of returning to work. A long break once a year is not enough to carry you.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Stress builds again once the job's demands return. Research on recovery shows the best effect comes from regular detachment from work, such as evenings and weekends, as well as the big trip.

Example: Someone returns from two weeks away feeling restored. By the third week back, the old tension has returned, because the daily pattern of overwork has not changed.

Apply it today: Plan one half-day or evening this week with no work contact, and treat it as a recovery appointment.

source.title: Do we recover from vacation? Meta-analysis of vacation effects on health and well-being
source.author: Jessica de Bloom and colleagues

ideas.title: Keep small high-powered magnets away from children
ideas.body: Swallowed magnets can pull together across the intestines and cause serious damage. Keep small magnet sets out of reach of children. If a child may have swallowed more than one, go to the emergency room right away.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Two magnets inside the gut can attract through tissue walls, squeezing it and causing holes, infections and emergency surgery. They may not cause obvious symptoms at first. That is why you should not wait for symptoms.

Example: A parent finds that several small magnets from a desk toy are missing after a toddler plays. She does not wait for symptoms and goes straight to hospital, where X-rays are done.

Apply it today: Check toys and desk gadgets for loose magnets today, and learn child first aid at a hands-on course.

ideas.title: A sure thing is overweighted compared with a very likely thing
ideas.body: The Allais paradox, named after economist Maurice Allais, shows that people often prefer a certain gain over a slightly better gamble, yet choose the better gamble when neither option is certain. The preference flips when certainty disappears.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Certainty has a special pull. Moving from nearly sure to completely sure feels bigger than the same step between two uncertain odds. This breaks the idea that choices follow expected value consistently, and it helps explain why people overpay for guarantees.

Example: Paying a high price for a warranty that removes the last bit of risk feels good, even though a slight cut in risk elsewhere would be worth the same amount of money.

Apply it today: Before paying to remove a small risk entirely, ask what that last step costs per bit of risk removed, and compare with where else you could spend it.

ideas.title: Fast rivers of air high above help planes fly east faster
ideas.body: The jet stream is a narrow band of fast winds about 9 to 12 kilometres up, mostly flowing west to east. It forms where warm tropical air meets cold polar air, bent by Earth's rotation. Planes use it to save time flying east.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: The bigger the temperature difference between two air masses, the stronger the pressure difference and the faster the wind. Rotation turns the flow into a stream along the boundary. It wanders in waves that shape weather below.

Example: Flights from North America to Europe are often shorter than the return trip. Pilots plan routes to ride the stream going east and avoid it going west.

Apply it today: Check a flight tracker for an east-to-west and a west-to-east flight on the same route and compare times.

ideas.title: Walking or cycling to work is linked to lower health risk
ideas.body: A UK study of hundreds of thousands of commuters found that people who cycled or walked to work had a lower risk of cardiovascular disease and early death than those who drove or took transport. It shows an association.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Commuting on foot or by bike adds regular activity without extra time. The study could not prove cause, because active commuters may differ in other ways, but the result fits the broader evidence that daily movement helps the heart.

Example: A clerk gets off the bus two stops early and walks the rest. It adds ten minutes each way and he reaches work awake.

Apply it today: If you commute, replace part of one trip with walking or cycling this week, even only the last stretch.

source.title: Association between active commuting and incident cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mortality: prospective cohort study
source.author: Carlos A. Celis-Morales and colleagues

ideas.title: Cordless blinds are safer, because looped cords can strangle children
ideas.body: Window blind cords and loops are a strangulation hazard for young children. Choose cordless blinds, or keep cords short and out of reach and move cribs and beds away from windows.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Toddlers can climb and get a loop around the neck in seconds, and the event is often silent. Removing the hazard works better than relying on supervision alone. Cordless products have become widely available.

Example: A couple replaces corded blinds in the nursery with cordless ones and moves the crib away from the window. They also tie remaining cords high on a wall hook.

Apply it today: Inspect the cords in your home today, and learn infant and child first aid at a hands-on class.

ideas.title: Time in nature lets tired attention recover
ideas.body: Rachel and Stephen Kaplan proposed attention restoration theory: focusing on tasks drains directed attention, while natural settings engage it gently, in what they called soft fascination, allowing it to recover.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Directed attention is limited and wears down with use. Environments that hold interest without effort, such as trees and water, give it a rest. Evidence for the effect is encouraging but mixed in size, so treat it as a likely helper, not a cure.

Example: After a long stretch of screen work, a short walk in a park may leave you more able to concentrate than a break scrolling your phone, which keeps demanding directed attention.

Apply it today: Take your next work break outdoors, even for ten minutes, and leave your phone in your pocket. Notice how your focus feels afterwards.

source.title: The restorative benefits of nature: Toward an integrative framework
source.author: Stephen Kaplan

ideas.title: Four tests tied a particular microbe to a particular disease
ideas.body: In the 1880s Robert Koch set out criteria to prove a microbe causes a disease: it must be found in the sick and not the healthy, grown in pure culture, cause the disease in a healthy host, and be found again in that host. He used them on anthrax and tuberculosis.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Before this, many thought diseases came from bad air. Showing a chain from one microbe to one illness made germ theory testable. Methods for growing bacteria on solid plates made pure cultures possible.

Example: The rules are not perfect: some microbes cannot be grown in a lab, and some carriers never get sick. Modern science supplements them with genetic evidence. Still, the logic of linking cause to effect is widely used.

Apply it today: Next time you read a health claim, ask whether anyone has shown a cause, not just that two things go together.

ideas.title: Venting anger tends to feed it, not drain it
ideas.body: A popular idea says that letting anger out, such as hitting a pillow, gets rid of it. In experiments, people who vented stayed angry and were more aggressive afterward than those who did something calming or distracting.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Venting keeps attention on the cause and rehearses the anger. Calming activities lower arousal, which lets anger fade. The researchers argued catharsis theory does not hold up, though talking calmly about a problem is different.

Example: After a bad meeting, a man slams his desk and rants to a colleague for twenty minutes and feels worse. His friend takes a walk and returns calm, ready to write a measured reply.

Apply it today: When you feel anger rising, take a slow walk or breathe slowly for a few minutes before you speak or write.

source.title: Does venting anger feed or extinguish the flame? Catharsis, rumination, distraction, anger, and aggressive responding
source.author: Brad J. Bushman

ideas.title: Fell through ice? Kick, reach forward and crawl out, then roll away
ideas.body: If you fall through ice, stay calm. Turn toward where you came from, put your arms on the ice, kick your legs hard to bring your body level, and pull yourself out. Roll away from the hole and then crawl to shore. Call emergency services and get warm.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: The ice you walked on held you, so it is likely strongest where you came from. Cold shock passes after about a minute, so you have time to act once your breathing settles. Rolling spreads your weight over a wider area.

Example: A fisherman breaks through near shore. He stops, gets his breath back, kicks to get his body flat, rolls out onto the ice and away, and then crawls to his friends. Afterwards he gets dry and warm quickly.

Apply it today: Carry ice picks around your neck on thin ice and tell someone your plans, and Take a hands-on first aid course from the Red Cross, St John Ambulance or a local provider, so your hands know what to do.

ideas.title: You may see objects only for their usual purpose
ideas.body: Karl Duncker's candle problem asks people to fix a candle to a wall using a box of tacks and matches. Many fail because they see the box only as a container. The answer is to tack the box to the wall as a shelf.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Functional fixedness is the habit of seeing an object only in its usual role. Once an item is in use as a container, it is hard to see it as a platform. Seeing the parts of a problem by their properties instead of their labels opens options.

Example: A cook without a rolling pin looks for a rolling pin. Someone who thinks in terms of what is needed, a smooth heavy cylinder, reaches for a clean bottle.

Apply it today: Pick a problem you are stuck on and list what you have on hand by physical properties, not names. Ask what each item could do besides its usual job.

ideas.title: Farmers plant based on today's price, so prices swing in cycles
ideas.body: The cobweb model explains boom and bust in markets where supply takes time to arrive. If pork prices are high now, farmers raise more pigs. A year later there are too many, prices crash, farmers cut back, and prices rise again. This is called the hog cycle.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Producers decide based on the current price, but sell at a future price. When everyone responds the same way, supply overshoots. The cycle damps if farmers learn or if supply is flexible, but can persist where delays are long.

Example: Similar patterns appear in shipbuilding, housing and graduate hiring, where training takes years. People entering a field because pay is high today may find the market flooded when they finish.

Apply it today: Before choosing a career or investment because it looks hot right now, ask how many others are reacting the same way and when they will arrive.

ideas.title: Time outdoors in childhood helps protect against short-sightedness
ideas.body: A trial in Chinese schools found that adding about 40 minutes of outdoor time each school day lowered the number of children who developed short-sightedness over three years. The cause is not fully understood.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Researchers suspect that bright outdoor light and looking at distant things help the eye grow properly. Time on close work, such as screens and books, is linked to more myopia. Regular eye tests still matter.

Example: A school adds an outdoor lesson break every day. Years later, fewer of its children need glasses than in nearby schools.

Apply it today: Get your child, or yourself, outside for a stretch of daylight today, and book an eye test if you have not had one in a while.

source.title: Effect of Time Spent Outdoors at School on the Development of Myopia Among Children in China
source.author: Mingguang He and colleagues

ideas.title: Rumbling in a hillside after heavy rain is a reason to leave at once
ideas.body: Landslides and debris flows can start with little warning on steep slopes after heavy rain. If you hear a rumble, see trees tilting, or notice sudden changes in a stream's flow, move quickly away from the path and upslope to high ground.
ideas.deeper:
Why it works: Saturated soil on slopes can give way and travel fast. Moving out of the path of flow, not downhill along it, improves the odds. Reporting the event allows others to be warned.

Example: After days of rain, a camper hears a low rumble above her tent and sees the stream turn muddy. She leaves at once, goes to higher ground to the side and calls emergency services.

Apply it today: Check landslide warnings for steep places you visit, and take a community emergency response or wilderness first aid course.
